Road to Hell

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Its flower time in the Namakwaland, but for locals, things don't seem that colourful!

Unique Selling Point:
After a decade long drought, farmers in the heart of the Namakwaland are now facing a whole new challenge

Summary:
It is not easy being a farmer in the heart of the country where it is arid and far removed from resources. Yet, 90% of all lamb products are produced here. After a nine year long strenuous drought, farmers are just getting to their feet again, but now, they face a whole new challenge; getting their product to the market... because logistics companies refuse to send their trucks to the farms. 4000km of vital road connecting farmers to towns and cities, are inaccessible. And when it rains, the roads turn into rivers, cutting farmers off from the world. If the province was granted just under 4 billion Rand to maintain these roads, why is this the state they're in?

Further information:
Sybil Visagie is a force to be reckoned with. A sheep farmer of the Hantam Karoo, she uses phrases most have probably not even heard before, like ‘Begrawe die donkies on die sand’. Contrary to what you may think it means, it actually refers to building barriers next to a gravel road to redirect water.
Because coming out of a near 9-year long drought, farmers in this part of the country face another major challenge, some say, may even be greater than the drought.

Fatal accidents, ambulances washing away in rivers that are not supposed to be there, trucking companies’ refusal to collect product from farms, children unable to get to school and tourist having to turn around, are all thanks to a the dilapidation of over 4000km of road in the Northern Cape.

First it was covid in the middle of drought, now that the drought is over, the roads pose another grave concern. Sybil used to farm 5000 sheep before the drought, she is down to 1200. And now, she had to take one entire farm out of production because transport companies refuse to collect product from a farm. “Die trokke skud letterlike middeldeur op die pad”. Only last year, Sybil spent over R190 thousand on replacement of tyres on her own bakkie. And the problem is echoed throughout the Namakwaland. While in research for this story, two farmers- who we visited while doing a story about the drought, called to tell us about the dire state of the roads.

The middle of August to the middle of October is peak tourism season for the Namakwaland. Some businesses only operate during this time and make provision for the next year. It is the world-famous flower season of the Namakwaland. The area had a lot of rain this year and it promises to be a spectacle of flowers. Only one problem, tourists are warned to bring 3 or 4 extra tyres for the journey. The impact the collapse of the road network will have on tourism and a great concern.

Sheep farming and tourism are the two major economic activities of the Namakwaland. Now, farmers can’t get their product to the market and tourists are warned about the state of the roads.

Unique Selling Point: After a decade long drought, farmers in the heart of the Namakwaland are now facing a whole new challenge Summary: It is not easy being a farmer in the heart of the country where it is arid and far removed from resources. Yet, 90% of all lamb products are produced here. After a nine year long strenuous drought, farmers are just getting to their feet again, but now, they face a whole new challenge; getting their product to the market... because logistics companies refuse to send their trucks to the farms. 4000km of vital road connecting farmers to towns and cities, are inaccessible. And when it rains, the roads turn into rivers, cutting farmers off from the world. If the province was granted just under 4 billion Rand to maintain these roads, why is this the state they're in? Further information: Sybil Visagie is a force to be reckoned with. A sheep farmer of the Hantam Karoo, she uses phrases most have probably not even heard before, like ‘Begrawe die donkies on die sand’. Contrary to what you may think it means, it actually refers to building barriers next to a gravel road to redirect water. Because coming out of a near 9-year long drought, farmers in this part of the country face another major challenge, some say, may even be greater than the drought. Fatal accidents, ambulances washing away in rivers that are not supposed to be there, trucking companies’ refusal to collect product from farms, children unable to get to school and tourist having to turn around, are all thanks to a the dilapidation of over 4000km of road in the Northern Cape. First it was covid in the middle of drought, now that the drought is over, the roads pose another grave concern. Sybil used to farm 5000 sheep before the drought, she is down to 1200. And now, she had to take one entire farm out of production because transport companies refuse to collect product from a farm. “Die trokke skud letterlike middeldeur op die pad”. Only last year, Sybil spent over R190 thousand on replacement of tyres on her own bakkie. And the problem is echoed throughout the Namakwaland. While in research for this story, two farmers- who we visited while doing a story about the drought, called to tell us about the dire state of the roads. The middle of August to the middle of October is peak tourism season for the Namakwaland. Some businesses only operate during this time and make provision for the next year. It is the world-famous flower season of the Namakwaland. The area had a lot of rain this year and it promises to be a spectacle of flowers. Only one problem, tourists are warned to bring 3 or 4 extra tyres for the journey. The impact the collapse of the road network will have on tourism and a great concern. Sheep farming and tourism are the two major economic activities of the Namakwaland. Now, farmers can’t get their product to the market and tourists are warned about the state of the roads. First it was covid in the middle of drought, now that the drought is over, the roads pose another grave concern. Sybil used to farm 5000 sheep before the drought, she is down to 1200. And now, she had to take one entire farm out of production because transport companies refuse to collect product from a farm. “Die trokke skud letterlike middeldeur op die pad”. Only last year, Sybil spent over R190 thousand on replacement of tyres on her own bakkie. And the problem is echoed throughout the Namakwaland. While in research for this story, two farmers- who we visited while doing a story about the drought, called to tell us about the dire state of the roads. The middle of August to the middle of October is peak tourism season for the Namakwaland. Some businesses only operate during this time and make provision for the next year. It is the world-famous flower season of the Namakwaland. The area had a lot of rain this year and it promises to be a spectacle of flowers. Only one problem, tourists are warned to bring 3 or 4 extra tyres for the journey. The impact the collapse of the road network will have on tourism and a great concern. Sheep farming and tourism are the two major economic activities of the Namakwaland. Now, farmers can’t get their product to the market and tourists are warned about the state of the roads.
